title: Topic Drill: Sentence Structure, Grammar and Punctuation (Set B)

items.stem:
The swim team meets at the community pool on Tuesday mornings. Coach Ruiz told Lena that she would swim the lead leg of the relay. Lena had hoped for that spot all season.

Which revision removes the unclear pronoun reference in the second sentence?
options: Coach Ruiz told Lena that she herself would swim the lead leg of the relay.
Coach Ruiz told her that Lena would swim the lead leg of the relay.
Coach Ruiz told Lena that they would swim the lead leg of the relay.
Coach Ruiz told Lena, “You will swim the lead leg of the relay this season.”
items.explanation: In the original, she could mean Coach Ruiz or Lena, so the reader cannot tell who swims the lead leg. Quoting the coach’s exact words with you removes the doubt. Adding herself still leaves two possible people. Switching to her moves the problem to a new pronoun with no clear referent. They has no plural antecedent at all.

items.stem:
A swim team parent is reading the pool’s posted rules before a late practice. The sign near the entrance is faded, but the main points are still clear. At the pool, they require every swimmer to shower before entering the water.

Which revision corrects the pronoun problem in the last sentence?
options: At the pool, it requires every swimmer to shower before entering the water.
At the pool, the managers they require every swimmer to shower before entering the water.
The pool requires every swimmer to shower before entering the water.
At the pool, you are required by them to shower before entering the water.
items.explanation: The pronoun they points to no one, since the sentence never names a person or group who makes the rules. Making the pool the subject is direct and clear. It requires still has no clear referent after a prepositional phrase. The managers they repeats the subject with a needless pronoun. The by them version stays vague and also shifts to you.

items.stem:
A swim team newsletter reminds families about meet-day routines. Doors open at six, and warm-ups begin at six thirty. Swimmers should check the lane assignments early because you can lose a warm-up slot by arriving late.

Which revision corrects the shift in the last sentence?
options: Swimmers should check the lane assignments early because they can lose a warm-up slot by arriving late.
Swimmers should check the lane assignments early because we can lose a warm-up slot by arriving late.
Swimmers should check the lane assignments early because it can lose a warm-up slot by arriving late.
Swimmers should check the lane assignments early because swimmers, they can lose a warm-up slot by arriving late.
items.explanation: The sentence begins in the third person with swimmers and then jumps to you, an inconsistent shift in person. Keeping they matches the subject. We introduces a speaker who was never part of the sentence. It points back to lane assignments, which cannot lose anything. Swimmers, they repeats the subject with a needless extra pronoun.

items.stem:
A swim team captain writes a friendly message to a teammate before the regional meet. We have trained hard since September, and the coach says our times are improving. Between you and I, the medley relay is our best chance for a trophy.

Which revision corrects the pronoun error in the last sentence?
options: Between you and myself, the medley relay is our best chance for a trophy.
Between you and me, the medley relay is our best chance for a trophy.
Between yourself and I, the medley relay is our best chance for a trophy.
Among you and I, the medley relay is our best chance for a trophy.
items.explanation: Between is a preposition, so both pronouns after it must be in the object case, you and me. I is a subject form. Myself is reflexive and has no earlier subject to refer back to. Yourself and I mixes a reflexive with a subject form, and among keeps the subject form I, so the case error survives.

items.stem:
The swim team is preparing for its first home meet of the season. The timers must reach their lanes by seven, and the starter will check each stopwatch. Mr. Okafor, whom the coach says is always punctual, will run the lane three watch.

Which revision corrects the pronoun error in the last sentence?
options: Mr. Okafor, who the coach says is always punctual, will run the lane three watch tonight.
Mr. Okafor, whomever the coach says is always punctual, will run the lane three watch.
Mr. Okafor, which the coach says is always punctual, will run the lane three watch.
Mr. Okafor, whose the coach says is always punctual, will run the lane three watch.
items.explanation: Inside the clause, the coach says is a parenthetical, and the pronoun is the subject of is always punctual, so it takes the subject form who. Whom is an object form and whomever carries the same mistake. Which refers to things, not people, and whose shows possession, which makes no sense before is.

items.stem:
The electric bike share is adding docks in the downtown district this spring. A map in the library lobby marks every planned site. There is three docks near the library and two near the old bridge.

Which revision corrects the error in the last sentence?
options: There is three dock near the library and two near the old bridge.
There was three docks near the library and two near the old bridge.
There are three docks near the library and two near the old bridge.
Their are three docks near the library and two near the old bridge.
items.explanation: In a sentence that begins with there, the verb agrees with the subject that follows it, and docks is plural, so are is needed. Making docks singular leaves is unmatched with three. Was only changes the tense and stays singular. Their is a possessive pronoun, a spelling slip for the adverb there, so it repairs nothing.

items.stem:
The electric bike share is surveying its riders about the new pricing plan. The questionnaires went out on Monday by email. Everyone on the rider panel have received a copy and has until Friday to reply.

Which revision corrects the agreement error in the last sentence?
options: Everyone on the rider panel are receiving a copy and has until Friday to reply.
Everyone on the rider panel were sent a copy and has until Friday to reply.
Everyone on the rider panels have received a copy and has until Friday to reply.
Everyone on the rider panel has received a copy and has until Friday to reply.
items.explanation: The subject everyone is singular no matter how many people it covers, so the verb must be has received, matching the second verb has. Are receiving and were sent are plural forms. Changing panel to panels only alters a prepositional object and leaves have attached to the singular pronoun everyone.

items.stem:
A bike share analyst is summarizing last quarter for the city council. The council wants to know whether summer promotions worked. The statistics in the monthly report shows that rides doubled in June.

Which revision corrects the error in subject-verb agreement?
options: The statistics in the monthly report is showing that rides doubled in June.
The statistics in the monthly report show that rides doubled in June.
The statistic in the monthly report show that rides doubled in June.
The statistics in the monthly report, shows that rides doubled in June.
items.explanation: Here statistics means a set of figures, which is plural, so the verb is show. Is showing is a singular verb. Cutting statistics to statistic leaves the plural verb show with a singular noun. A comma between the subject and the verb does not fix the mismatch and also separates a subject from its verb for no reason.

items.stem:
A bike share newsletter profiles its most dedicated riders. Many of them commute year-round and log every trip in the app. Janelle is the only one of the riders who have logged all three hundred and sixty trips this year.

Which revision corrects the agreement error?
options: Janelle is the only one of the riders who have logged all three hundred and sixty trips this year.
Janelle are the only one of the riders who have logged all three hundred and sixty trips this year.
Janelle is the only one of the riders who has logged all three hundred and sixty trips this year.
Janelle is the only one of the riders who logging all three hundred and sixty trips this year.
items.explanation: In the phrase the only one of, the relative pronoun who refers to one, not to riders, so it takes the singular verb has. The wrong choices keep the plural have, change the main verb to are, or use a participle that is not a complete verb, leaving the clause without a finite verb.

items.stem:
The bike share held a public comment night at the library. Staff collected cards from the audience and sorted them by topic. A number of riders has asked for longer rental windows on weekends.

Which revision corrects the error in the last sentence?
options: The number of riders have asked for longer rental windows on weekends.
A number of riders is asking for longer rental windows on weekends.
A number of rider has asked for longer rental windows on weekends.
A number of riders have asked for longer rental windows on weekends.
items.explanation: The phrase a number of means several, so the plural noun riders controls the verb, which should be have. The number of would take a singular verb and changes the meaning. Is asking stays singular. Dropping the s from rider leaves has with a noun that no longer matches a number of.

items.stem:
A recycling center newsletter describes its weekly routine for new customers. Trucks arrive at dawn, and workers unload them by hand. Residents dropped off glass on Monday, and the staff sorts it by color before noon.

Which revision corrects the inconsistent verb tense in the last sentence?
options: Residents drop off glass on Monday, and the staff sorted it by color before noon.
Residents drop off glass on Monday, and the staff sorts it by color before noon each week.
Residents dropped off glass on Monday, and the staff will sort it by color before noon.
Residents have dropped off glass on Monday, and the staff sorts it by color before noon.
items.explanation: The passage describes a regular routine in the present tense, arrive and unload, so both verbs in the last sentence belong in the present: drop off and sorts. Sorted keeps one verb in the past. Dropped off with will sort mixes past and future. Have dropped off pairs a present perfect with a habitual day, which does not fit a routine.

items.stem:
A recycling center is writing a short history for its annual report. The center now serves four towns and employs twenty people. Marta Dunn was a retired teacher who starts the program in 1994 with one trailer and a borrowed truck.

Which revision corrects the verb tense in the last sentence?
options: Marta Dunn was a retired teacher who started the program in 1994 with one trailer and a borrowed truck.
Marta Dunn was a retired teacher who had start the program in 1994 with one trailer and a borrowed truck.
Marta Dunn was a retired teacher who would start the program in 1994 with one trailer and a borrowed truck.
Marta Dunn was a retired teacher who has started the program in 1994 with one trailer and a borrowed truck.
items.explanation: The date 1994 and the verb was place the action in the past, so the relative clause needs the simple past, started. Had start is not a real verb form. Would start suggests a habit or a plan rather than a single event. Has started is a present perfect, which cannot be used with a specific past year.

items.stem:
A volunteer at a recycling center writes an incident note for the supervisor. The hazard room is for batteries, paint cans and other items that cannot go in the bins. Yesterday a volunteer found a battery in the paper bin and carries it to the hazard room.

Which revision corrects the shift in tense in the last sentence?
options: Yesterday a volunteer found a battery in the paper bin and will carry it to the hazard room.
Yesterday a volunteer found a battery in the paper bin and carried it to the hazard room right away.
Yesterday a volunteer found a battery in the paper bin and has carried it to the hazard room.
Yesterday a volunteer found a battery in the paper bin and would carry it to the hazard room.
items.explanation: The word yesterday and the verb found put both actions in the past, so the second verb should be carried. Will carry points to the future. Has carried is a present perfect that clashes with a specific day in the past. Would carry suggests a habit or a condition instead of a single completed act.

items.stem:
The recycling center installed a new compactor at the end of last year. Managers want the annual report to show what changed since then. Since the new compactor arrived, the center process more loads each week.

Which revision corrects the verb in the last sentence?
options: Since the new compactor arrived, the center will process more loads each week.
Since the new compactor arrived, the center had processed more loads each week.
Since the new compactor arrived, the center processing more loads each week.
Since the new compactor arrived, the center has processed more loads each week.
items.explanation: A sentence that begins with since and describes change continuing up to now calls for the present perfect, has processed. Will process looks forward, not back. Had processed is a past perfect with no later past event to anchor it. Processing alone is a fragment because it lacks a helping verb.

items.stem:
A recycling center closed early on Friday because of a power outage. The manager is explaining the plan to the weekend crew. The supervisor said the center would reopen as soon as the crew finishes sweeping the yard.

Which revision corrects the verb tense in the last sentence?
options: The supervisor said the center would reopen as soon as the crew finished sweeping the entire yard.
The supervisor said the center would reopen as soon as the crew will finish sweeping the yard.
The supervisor said the center would reopen as soon as the crew would finish sweeping the yard.
The supervisor said the center would reopen as soon as the crew is finishing sweeping the yard.
items.explanation: Because the main verbs said and would reopen are in the past frame, the time clause must also be past: finished. Will finish and is finishing keep it in the present or future. Would finish inside an as soon as clause is not standard, since the clause already sits in the past through the first verb.

items.stem:
A school science fair newsletter profiles the exhibits in the gym. Tables line both walls, and each project has a display board. Covered in baking soda, the judges admired the volcano model for its realistic crater.

Which revision corrects the dangling modifier in the last sentence?
options: The judges, covered in baking soda, admired the volcano model for its realistic crater.
Covered in baking soda, admiration for the realistic crater came from the judges.
Covered in baking soda, the volcano model impressed the judges with its realistic crater.
While covered in baking soda, the judges admired the volcano model for its crater.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes the volcano model, so the model must be the next noun. The judges were not covered in baking soda, and the revised version that moves the phrase beside them says so. Making admiration the subject leaves the phrase attached to a word it cannot describe, and adding while changes nothing about who is covered.

items.stem:
The science fair rules are posted outside the gym for students and parents. The judging committee wrote them carefully this year. The judges only scored projects that included a written hypothesis.

Which revision corrects the misplaced modifier in the last sentence?
options: The judges scored only projects that included a written hypothesis.
The judges scored projects only that included a written hypothesis.
The judges scored projects that only included a written hypothesis.
Only the judges scored projects that included a written hypothesis.
items.explanation: The word only should sit directly before the words it limits, here projects that included a written hypothesis. Placing it before scored suggests the judges did nothing else with the projects. Moving it after projects is awkward and splits the phrase. Putting it before included suggests the projects had nothing but a hypothesis. Opening with only the judges limits who scored.

items.stem:
A seventh grader describes her bean-plant experiment in a science fair report. She tested three kinds of soil over five weeks and measured each plant daily. After testing three kinds of soil, a graph showed which one grew the tallest beans.

Which revision corrects the dangling modifier?
options: After testing three kinds of soil, which one grew the tallest beans was shown in a graph.
After testing three kinds of soil, the graph that Priya made showed which one grew tallest.
Testing three kinds of soil, a graph showed which one grew the tallest beans.
After testing three kinds of soil, Priya made a graph showing which one grew the tallest beans.
items.explanation: The opening phrase needs a person who did the testing, and a graph cannot test soil. Naming Priya as the subject repairs the sentence. The version that makes a clause the subject and the one that makes the graph the subject still leave the phrase attached to the wrong noun. Dropping after does not solve the problem.

items.stem:
Mia is writing an account of judging day for the school paper. The judges moved from table to table with clipboards and asked questions. Mia watched the judge with a magnifying glass examine her poster.

Which revision removes the ambiguity from the last sentence?
options: Mia, with a magnifying glass, watched the judge examine her poster.
Mia watched the judge use a magnifying glass to examine her poster.
With a magnifying glass, Mia watched the judge examine her poster.
Mia watched the judge examine her poster, which had a magnifying glass.
items.explanation: In the original, with a magnifying glass could describe the judge, Mia, or the poster. Saying the judge used the glass to examine the poster shows who held it. The other versions attach the phrase to Mia or to the poster, so the reader still has to guess who or what had the magnifying glass.

items.stem:
A team from the school science fair built a model fountain with a small pump. The pump failed twice during testing. Frustrated by the broken pump, the fountain model was abandoned by the team on Thursday.

Which revision corrects the dangling modifier?
options: Frustrated by the broken pump, abandonment of the fountain model came on Thursday.
The team’s fountain model, frustrated by the broken pump, was abandoned on Thursday.
Frustrated by the broken pump, the team abandoned the fountain model on Thursday afternoon.
Because frustrated by the broken pump, the fountain model was abandoned on Thursday.
items.explanation: Frustrated describes a person, so the team must follow the comma as the subject. A model cannot feel frustration, which is the problem with the original and with the version that moves the phrase beside the model. Making abandonment the subject names no one, and because frustrated is not a grammatical clause opener.

items.stem:
A neighborhood clinic is advertising its annual fundraiser on a flyer. The event takes place in the church hall on the second Saturday of June. The fundraiser will feature a silent auction, live music, and children can play games.

Which revision corrects the error in parallel structure?
options: The fundraiser will feature a silent auction, live music, and having games for children.
The fundraiser will feature a silent auction, live music, and the children are playing games.
The fundraiser will feature a silent auction, live music, and to play games with the children.
The fundraiser will feature a silent auction, live music, and children’s games.
items.explanation: The series after feature needs three matching noun phrases: a silent auction, live music and children’s games. A clause such as children can play games, a gerund phrase, an infinitive phrase, or a clause with a subject and verb each break the pattern and change the grammatical form of the last item.

items.stem:
The clinic’s volunteer coordinator is writing instructions for ticket buyers. Tickets are limited to two hundred, so early buyers have the best chance. Neighbors can either buy a ticket online or by stopping at the front desk.

Which revision corrects the faulty parallelism in the last sentence?
options: Neighbors can either buy a ticket online or at the front desk.
Neighbors can buy a ticket either online or at the front desk.
Neighbors can either buy a ticket online or stopping at the front desk.
Neighbors can buy a ticket either online or by stopping at the front desk.
items.explanation: Either and or must introduce matching elements. In the key, online and at the front desk are both adverbial phrases that follow buy a ticket. Placing either before buy sets a verb against a phrase. Pairing online with stopping mixes an adverb with a gerund, and pairing online with by stopping still mixes an adverb with a gerund phrase.

items.stem:
A clinic board member is reporting results from the fundraiser to the neighborhood association. Last year’s pancake breakfast was popular, and this year’s dinner drew more families. Ticket sales this year are higher than last year.

Which revision corrects the faulty comparison in the last sentence?
options: Ticket sales this year are higher than they were last year.
Ticket sales this year are higher then they were last year.
Ticket sales this year are more higher than they were last year.
Ticket sales this year are higher than the year before ago.
items.explanation: The original compares ticket sales with a year, two unlike things. Adding they were makes it compare sales with sales. Then is a word for time, not for comparison. More higher doubles the comparative. The year before ago is a garbled phrase that still compares sales with a year and adds a redundant time word.

items.stem:
A neighborhood clinic planning committee is posting its to-do list in the break room. The date is set, and the food donors are confirmed. The committee will book the hall, print the flyers, and the menu must be approved by the chef.

Which revision corrects the error in parallel structure?
options: The committee will book the hall, print the flyers, and approving the menu.
The committee will book the hall, print the flyers, and the approval of the menu.
The committee will book the hall, print the flyers, and approve the menu with the chef.
The committee will book the hall, print the flyers, and to approve the menu.
items.explanation: Three verbs follow the subject committee, so each should be in the same form after will: book, print and approve. A gerund, a noun phrase, or an infinitive in the last position breaks the series. The passive clause in the original adds a new subject and verb, so it is not parallel either.

items.stem:
A local newspaper is preparing a short profile of the neighborhood clinic’s director. She has led the clinic for twelve years and organizes the fundraiser each spring. The clinic’s director is energetic, well organized, and has a reputation for kindness.

Which revision corrects the error in parallel structure?
options: The clinic’s director is energetic, well organized, and kind.
The clinic’s director is energetic, well organized, and being kind.
The clinic’s director is energetic, well organized, and kindness is her reputation.
The clinic’s director is energetic, well organized, and she is known for being kind.
items.explanation: After is, the series needs three adjectives: energetic, well organized and kind. A verb phrase with has a reputation breaks the pattern. A gerund such as being kind, a full clause with its own subject, and a clause introduced by she is known each change the grammatical form of the last item.

items.stem:
A community theater program includes a short note about its costume shop. The shop is housed behind the box office and keeps a full-time staff. The shop’s head seamstress who has worked there for thirty years taught the apprentices to hem by hand.

Which revision punctuates the last sentence correctly?
options: The shop’s head seamstress, who has worked there for thirty years taught the apprentices to hem by hand.
The shop’s head seamstress who has worked there for thirty years, taught the apprentices to hem by hand.
The shop’s head seamstress, who has worked there for thirty years, taught the apprentices to hem by hand.
The shop’s head, seamstress, who has worked there for thirty years, taught the apprentices to hem by hand.
items.explanation: The shop has one head seamstress, so the who clause adds extra information and needs a pair of commas around it. A single comma before or after the clause leaves it half set off. The last version puts a comma between head and seamstress, which splits a title in the wrong place.

items.stem:
A costume shop manager is explaining a change to the cast of a winter play. The dancers complained during the first fitting. The velvet cape was too heavy for the dancers so the shop switched to a lighter wool.

Which revision punctuates the last sentence correctly?
options: The velvet cape was too heavy, for the dancers so the shop switched to a lighter wool.
The velvet cape was too heavy for the dancers so, the shop switched to a lighter wool.
The velvet cape was too heavy for the dancers, so the shop, switched to a lighter wool.
The velvet cape was too heavy for the dancers, so the shop switched to a lighter wool.
items.explanation: Two main clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction so need a comma before it, right after dancers. A comma placed earlier, after heavy, interrupts the first clause. A comma after so separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces. A comma after shop splits the second clause’s subject from its verb.

items.stem:
The costume shop owns hundreds of garments, but only forty were rented out last week. Each rental is logged in a ledger by the front desk. The costumes, that were rented to the high school were returned on Monday.

Which revision punctuates the last sentence correctly?
options: The costumes, which were rented to the high school were returned on Monday.
The costumes that were rented to the high school were returned on Monday morning.
The costumes that were rented to the high school, were returned on Monday.
The costumes, that were rented to the high school, were returned on Monday.
items.explanation: Only some of the shop’s costumes went to the high school, so the clause tells which ones and is essential. It takes no commas and starts with that. Commas around it would suggest all the costumes were rented there. Using which with one comma, or a lone comma after school, separates the subject from its verb.

items.stem:
A costume shop memo is posted above the sewing machines. The play opens in two weeks, and every hem must be finished soon. The tailor wants the hems done by hand not by machine.

Which revision punctuates the last sentence correctly?
options: The tailor wants the hems done by hand, not by machine.
The tailor wants the hems done, by hand not by machine.
The tailor wants the hems done by hand not, by machine.
The tailor wants the hems done by hand; not by machine.
items.explanation: A contrasting phrase that begins with not is set off from the rest of the sentence by a comma, here placed after hand. A comma earlier splits the verb phrase. A comma after not separates the word from what it modifies. A semicolon needs a full clause on each side, and not by machine is only a phrase.

items.stem:
A theater newsletter is running a short history of its costume shop. The shop began in a basement and moved to its present location after a donation. The shop opened on March 3, 2019 and has served four local theaters since.

Which revision punctuates the last sentence correctly?
options: The shop opened on March 3 2019, and has served four local theaters since.
The shop opened on March 3, 2019, and has served four local theaters since.
The shop opened on March, 3, 2019 and has served four local theaters since.
The shop opened on March 3, 2019; and has served four local theaters since.
items.explanation: A full date inside a sentence has a comma between the day and year and another after the year, so 2019 is followed by a comma. The first wrong choice drops the comma after the day. The second puts a comma between the month and the day and leaves out the one after the year. A semicolon cannot precede and when the second part lacks its own subject.

items.stem:
A hiking club is printing a trail guide for the summit route. The route is long, and the weather changes quickly above the tree line. Pack three essentials for the summit trail, water, a map, and a rain jacket.

Which revision punctuates the last sentence correctly?
options: Pack three essentials for the summit trail; water, a map, and a rain jacket.
Pack three essentials for the summit trail. Water, a map, and a rain jacket.
Pack three essentials for the summit trail water, a map, and a rain jacket.
Pack three essentials for the summit trail: water, a map, and a rain jacket.
items.explanation: A colon after a complete statement introduces the list that explains it, and the statement here ends at trail. A semicolon needs a full clause after it, and the list is not one. A period leaves the list as a fragment. Removing the mark entirely runs the statement and the list together.

items.stem:
The morning hiking group and the afternoon group share one guide, so schedules matter. A trail ranger is posting the plan for the first weekend. The morning group left at six, meanwhile the afternoon group packed lunches at the lodge.

Which revision corrects the punctuation error in the last sentence?
options: The morning group left at six, meanwhile, the afternoon group packed lunches at the lodge.
The morning group left at six: meanwhile, the afternoon group packed lunches at the lodge.
The morning group left at six; meanwhile, the afternoon group packed lunches at the lodge.
The morning group left at six meanwhile; the afternoon group packed lunches at the lodge.
items.explanation: Meanwhile is a conjunctive adverb, so it cannot join two main clauses with only a comma. A semicolon comes before it and a comma after it. Using a comma before it leaves a splice. A colon does not fit because the second clause does not explain the first, and putting the semicolon after meanwhile splits the adverb from the clause it begins.

items.stem:
A trail maintenance volunteer is writing a work request for the park office. Several parts of the ridge trail have worn down over the winter. Several features of the trail need repair, for example the footbridge has a loose rail and the signs have faded.

Which revision corrects the punctuation error in the last sentence?
options: Several features of the trail need repair, for example, the footbridge has a loose rail and the signs have faded.
Several features of the trail need repair; for example, the footbridge has a loose rail and the signs have faded.
Several features of the trail need repair; for example, the footbridge has a loose rail and, the signs have faded.
Several features of the trail need repair for example; the footbridge has a loose rail and the signs have faded.
items.explanation: For example, introducing a full clause, works like a conjunctive adverb, so a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it. A comma before it creates a splice. A stray comma after and, which splits the conjunction from its clause, is also wrong, and moving the semicolon after example cuts the phrase off from the clause it introduces.

items.stem:
A hiking guidebook describes the best views along a coastal path. The path is five miles long and takes about three hours. The trail has three viewpoints; the waterfall, the meadow, and the ridge.

Which revision punctuates the last sentence correctly?
options: The trail has three viewpoints. The waterfall, the meadow, and the ridge.
The trail has three viewpoints the waterfall, the meadow, and the ridge.
The trail has three viewpoints: the waterfall, the meadow, and the ridge.
The trail has three viewpoints: the waterfall: the meadow: and the ridge.
items.explanation: The words after viewpoints are a list, not a complete clause, so a semicolon is wrong. A single colon after the complete statement introduces the list. A period leaves the list as a fragment. Dropping the mark fuses the list to the statement, and extra colons between items misuse the mark.

items.stem:
A hiking club is scheduling its volunteer trail days for the summer. Each date comes with a location, and members sign up for the day they prefer. The club will work on Saturday, June 7, at Fern Creek, Sunday, June 8, at Cedar Point, and Saturday, June 14, at the lookout.

Which revision punctuates the list so that each work day is clear?
options: The club will work on Saturday; June 7, at Fern Creek, Sunday; June 8, at Cedar Point, and Saturday; June 14, at the lookout.
The club will work on Saturday, June 7, at Fern Creek: Sunday, June 8, at Cedar Point: and Saturday, June 14, at the lookout.
The club will work on Saturday, June 7, at Fern Creek, Sunday, June 8, at Cedar Point; and Saturday, June 14, at the lookout.
The club will work on Saturday, June 7, at Fern Creek; Sunday, June 8, at Cedar Point; and Saturday, June 14, at the lookout.
items.explanation: Each item holds several commas, so semicolons must mark the major breaks between the three work days. Placing semicolons between a weekday and its date splits the items wrongly. Colons are not used to separate list items. Using only one semicolon before the last item leaves the first two days running together.

items.stem:
A coffee roaster is announcing a grand opening in the neighborhood paper. Jon and Mira bought the building together and spent a year renovating it. Jon’s and Mira’s new roastery opens on Friday at nine.

Which revision shows joint ownership correctly?
options: Jon and Mira’s new roastery opens on Friday at nine.
Jon and Miras new roastery opens on Friday at nine.
Jons and Miras’ new roastery opens on Friday at nine.
Jon and Mira’s’ new roastery opens on Friday at nine.
items.explanation: When two people own one thing together, only the last name takes the possessive: Jon and Mira’s. Putting an apostrophe on both names suggests separate roasteries. Dropping the apostrophe leaves no possessive at all. Misplacing the apostrophes before the s, or adding a second one, produces forms that do not exist.

items.stem:
The coffee roaster holds a public cupping every Saturday, where visitors taste several roasts side by side. Staff arrange the cups in rows of six. Who’s cup is the one left on the cupping table by the window?

Which revision corrects the error in the last sentence?
options: Whos cup is the one left on the cupping table by the window?
Who is cup is the one left on the cupping table by the window?
Whose cup is the one left on the cupping table by the window?
Whose’ cup is the one left on the cupping table by the window?
items.explanation: Who’s is a contraction of who is, which makes no sense before cup. The possessive form whose asks who owns the cup. Whos has no apostrophe and is not a word. Who is cup repeats the contraction’s problem in full. Whose’ adds an apostrophe that possessive pronouns never take.

items.stem:
A coffee roaster’s flyer promotes a new Ethiopian roast. The tasting is free, but visitors must have a stamped ticket. If your planning to try the new roast, you’re ticket must be stamped at the door.

Which revision corrects both errors in the last sentence?
options: If your planning to try the new roast, your ticket must be stamped at the door.
If you’re planning to try the new roast, your ticket must be stamped at the door.
If you’re planning to try the new roast, you’re ticket must be stamped at the door.
If your planning to try the new roast, you’re ticket must be stamped at the door.
items.explanation: The first blank needs the contraction you’re, meaning you are, and the second needs the possessive your, because the ticket belongs to the reader. The original swaps them. Each wrong choice either keeps the possessive where the contraction belongs, keeps the contraction where the possessive belongs, or reverses the pair.

items.stem:
A roastery owner is helping two crews sort burlap sacks in the warehouse. The sacks look alike, so each crew marked its own. The red sack is ours, and the blue sack is their’s.

Which revision corrects the error in the last sentence?
options: The red sack is ours, and the blue sack is there’s.
The red sack is ours, and the blue sack is theirs’.
The red sack is ours, and the blue sack is thiers.
The red sack is ours, and the blue sack is theirs.
items.explanation: Possessive pronouns such as ours and theirs never take an apostrophe, because they already show ownership. There’s is a contraction of there is. Theirs’ adds an apostrophe that does not belong. Thiers is a misspelling that reverses the vowels. Writers often add an apostrophe out of habit, but pronouns such as his, hers, ours and yours stand alone.

items.stem:
A roastery’s head roaster describes a typical shift in a trade magazine profile. The drum is loaded before sunrise, and the first batch is ready by eight. After a long days work, the roasting crew cleans the drum and swaps the chaff trays.

Which revision corrects the possessive error in the last sentence?
options: After a long day’s work, the roasting crew cleans the drum and swaps the chaff trays.
After a long days’ work, the roasting crew cleans the drum and swaps the chaff trays.
After a long days’s work, the roasting crew cleans the drum and swaps the chaff trays.
After a long day work, the roasting crew cleans the drum and swaps the chaff trays.
items.explanation: The phrase refers to the work of one day, so the singular possessive day’s is correct. Days’ would mean several days, and the wording does not say so. Days’s mixes a plural with a singular ending. Dropping the apostrophe entirely loses the possessive relationship between day and work.

items.stem:
A coffee roaster’s care card is packed with every bag of beans. The card explains how to keep the roast fresh at home. If the lid is not tightened, the beans will loose their aroma within a week.

Which revision corrects the word choice error in the last sentence?
options: If the lid is not tightened, the beans will loosen their aroma within a week.
If the lid is not tightened, the beans will losing their aroma within a week.
If the lid is not tightened, the beans will lose their aroma within a week.
If the lid is not tightened, the beans will lost their aroma within a week.
items.explanation: Lose, with one o, is the verb meaning to no longer have something, and it follows will. Loose is an adjective meaning not tight. Loosen is a verb meaning to make less tight, which changes the meaning. Losing and lost are verb forms that cannot follow will.

items.stem:
A neighborhood clinic is selling baked goods at its spring fundraiser. A volunteer is writing the table sign. The lemon bars are a perfect compliment to the strong coffee from the local roaster.

Which revision corrects the word choice error in the last sentence?
options: The lemon bars are a perfect complimentary to the strong coffee from the local roaster.
The lemon bars are a perfect complimenting to the strong coffee from the local roaster.
The lemon bars are a perfect complements to the strong coffee from the local roaster.
The lemon bars are a perfect complement to the strong coffee from the local roaster.
items.explanation: Complement means something that completes or goes well with another, which is the sense here. Compliment is a kind remark. Complimentary is an adjective that means free or flattering, and complimenting is a verb form. A perfect complements breaks the number agreement between the article and noun.

items.stem:
The clinic’s fundraiser committee is meeting to finalize the auction plan. The chair has asked each member for one decision before the next meeting. The committee voted to precede with the auction plan after reviewing the budget.

Which revision corrects the word choice error in the last sentence?
options: The committee voted to proceed with the auction plan after reviewing the budget.
The committee voted to procede with the auction plan after reviewing the budget.
The committee voted to preceed with the auction plan after reviewing the budget.
The committee voted to proceeds with the auction plan after reviewing the budget.
items.explanation: Proceed means to go forward, which fits a vote to continue with a plan. Precede means to come before. The spellings procede and preceed do not exist. Proceeds is a verb ending that cannot follow to, and it also looks like the noun for money raised.

items.stem:
A swim team registration desk posts a notice on the pool door. Because of high demand, the team filled its roster last week. At this point in time, the swim team has no openings left.

Which revision removes the wordiness from the last sentence?
options: At the present time right now, the swim team has no openings left.
Right now, the swim team has no openings left.
At this point in time, the swim team has no remaining open openings left.
In this day and age at present, the swim team has no openings left.
items.explanation: At this point in time is a long way of saying now, and now or right now carries the meaning in two words. The wrong choices stack more empty phrases, such as at the present time with right now, or repeat the idea with remaining open openings left, so they stay wordy and add nothing to the meaning.

items.stem:
A bike share company is describing its new app in a customer email. The app replaced a clunky version that confused many riders. The new app is simple and easy to use and it also does not require much effort to learn.

Which revision is the most concise without losing meaning?
options: The new app is simple to use and quick to learn.
The new app is simple and easy to use, and it is also very simple to learn.
The new app is both simple and easy and also not hard to use and learn.
The new app is simple, easy, and uncomplicated to use and also to learn.
items.explanation: Simple and easy mean nearly the same thing, and not requiring much effort to learn is a roundabout way of saying quick to learn. The key keeps both ideas in eleven words. The other versions keep repeating simple, easy and not hard, or add also and both, so they remain padded with words that carry no new information.

items.stem:
A hiking club leader is writing a cancellation notice for members. The weekend outing was meant to cover the full lower loop. Due to the fact that it rained for two days, the hike was postponed until next month.

Which revision is the most concise and still clear?
options: Due to the fact that of the rain, the hike was postponed until next month.
On account of the fact that it was raining, the hike was postponed until next month.
As a result of the fact that rain fell, the hike was postponed until next month.
Because it rained for two days, the hike was postponed until next month.
items.explanation: Due to the fact that is a wordy stand-in for because, which says the same thing in one word. The other versions keep a filler phrase such as on account of the fact that, or as a result of the fact that, and the first also garbles the grammar with that of. Only the key cuts the filler.

items.stem:
A swim team coach is drafting a paragraph for the parent handbook. The draft uses three short sentences in a row. The swim team practices at dawn. The practices are held at the Maple Street pool. The practices help swimmers build endurance.

Which choice best combines the three sentences into one clear sentence?
options: The swim team practices at dawn, the practices are held at the Maple Street pool, and they help swimmers build endurance.
Held at dawn at the Maple Street pool, the swim team’s practices help swimmers build endurance.
The swim team practices at dawn, and being held at the Maple Street pool, helps swimmers build endurance.
The swim team practices at dawn and the practices are held at the Maple Street pool they help swimmers build endurance.
items.explanation: The key turns two sentences into a modifying phrase and keeps one main clause, so the repeated subject practices appears only once. The version with commas strings three clauses together as a splice. The second wrong choice leaves a dangling phrase with no subject. The last choice fuses clauses with no punctuation.

items.stem:
A recycling center is revising its drop-off sign so that it reads smoothly. The sign now lists the materials in three choppy lines. The recycling center accepts glass. It also accepts cans. It does not accept ceramics.

Which choice best combines the three sentences?
options: The recycling center accepts glass and cans, because it does not accept ceramics.
The recycling center accepts glass, cans it does not accept ceramics.
The recycling center accepts glass and cans but not ceramics.
Accepting glass and cans, ceramics are not accepted by the recycling center.
items.explanation: The key joins the two accepted items with and and sets the exception off with but, so the contrast is plain. Because suggests that refusing ceramics causes the center to take glass and cans, a false link. The third choice is fused. The fourth opens with a phrase that attaches to ceramics, a dangling modifier.

items.stem:
A theater program committee is polishing a note about its costume shop. The draft states the facts in three separate sentences. The costume shop is owned by Ms. Alvarez. Ms. Alvarez is a retired actor. She opened the shop in 2015.

Which choice best combines the three sentences into one?
options: Ms. Alvarez is a retired actor, she owns the costume shop which she opened in 2015.
Ms. Alvarez, a retired actor owns the costume shop, which she opened in 2015.
A retired actor, the costume shop was opened in 2015 by Ms. Alvarez.
Ms. Alvarez, a retired actor, owns the costume shop, which she opened in 2015.
items.explanation: The key renames Ms. Alvarez with an appositive set off by two commas and adds a which clause for the opening date. The first wrong choice is a comma splice. The second leaves out the comma after actor, so the appositive is not closed. The last choice says the shop itself is a retired actor, a dangling modifier.

items.stem:
A coffee roaster is inspecting a storage bin before a large order goes out. The inspector wrote a short note for the owner after opening the bin. Half of the beans in the bin is stale and must be discarded.

Which revision corrects the error in subject-verb agreement?
options: Half of the beans in the bin are stale and must be discarded.
Half of the beans in the bin was stale and must be discarded.
Half of the beans in the bin has gone stale and must be discarded.
Half of the bean in the bin are stale and must be discarded.
items.explanation: With a fraction such as half, the verb agrees with the noun in the of phrase, and beans is plural, so are is needed. Was and has gone are singular verbs. Changing beans to bean makes the noun singular but keeps the plural verb are, so the agreement breaks the other way.

items.stem:
A neighborhood clinic held a thank-you lunch after its fundraiser. Forty people helped set up tables, count tickets and clean the hall. The clinic director thanked we volunteers for our hard work.

Which revision corrects the pronoun error in the last sentence?
options: The clinic director thanked ourselves volunteers for our hard work.
The clinic director thanked us volunteers for our hard work.
The clinic director thanked volunteers like we for our hard work.
The clinic director thanked we, the volunteers, for our hard work.
items.explanation: The pronoun is the object of thanked, so it takes the object form us, as in thanked us. We is a subject form. Ourselves is reflexive and has no matching subject. Like we keeps the subject form after a preposition, and setting off the volunteers with commas does not change the case of we.

items.stem:
A hiking club posted a note about a footbridge on the Cedar Point trail. The crew finished the rebuild last summer. Last summer the trail crew rebuilt the footbridge, and hikers cross it safely ever since.

Which revision corrects the verb in the last sentence?
options: Last summer the trail crew rebuilt the footbridge, and hikers cross it safely ever since.
Last summer the trail crew rebuilt the footbridge, and hikers crossed it safely ever since.
Last summer the trail crew rebuilt the footbridge, and hikers have crossed it safely ever since.
Last summer the trail crew rebuilt the footbridge, and hikers had crossed it safely ever since.
items.explanation: Ever since describes an action that started in the past and continues now, which calls for the present perfect, have crossed. Cross is a simple present and ignores the starting point. Crossed treats the action as finished. Had crossed needs a later past event to anchor it, and none is given.

items.stem:
A coffee roaster’s apprentice is training on warehouse inventory. A senior employee left a note about the sacks of green beans. Stacked beside the roaster, the apprentice counted the burlap sacks before lunch.

Which revision corrects the modifier error in the last sentence?
options: The apprentice, stacked beside the roaster, counted the burlap sacks before lunch.
The apprentice carefully counted all of the burlap sacks stacked beside the roaster before lunch.
Stacked beside the roaster, counting the burlap sacks was the apprentice’s job before lunch.
Counting the burlap sacks, the apprentice stacked beside the roaster before lunch.
items.explanation: Stacked describes the sacks, so the phrase must sit next to them. In the original it opens the sentence and attaches to the apprentice, who was not stacked. Setting it off after apprentice gives the same wrong meaning. Starting with counting makes the dangling phrase worse by tying it to a task, not to the sacks.

items.stem:
The school science fair rules list what every entry must contain. Judges check the rules before awarding any ribbon. Contestants must submit a hypothesis, a procedure, and they must include a data table.

Which revision corrects the error in parallel structure?
options: Contestants must submit a hypothesis, a procedure, and including a data table.
Contestants must submit a hypothesis, a procedure, and to include a data table.
Contestants must submit a hypothesis, a procedure, and a data table.
Contestants must submit a hypothesis, a procedure, and a data table that they must include.
items.explanation: The series after submit should have three matching nouns: a hypothesis, a procedure and a data table. A clause with its own subject, a gerund phrase, or an infinitive phrase breaks the pattern. The last version keeps the noun but adds a clause that repeats the requirement, which is wordy and redundant.

items.stem:
An electric bike share posted a courtesy sign at each dock. The sign is short and is aimed at riders returning bikes at night. Riders please lock your bikes at the dock before leaving.

Which revision punctuates the sentence correctly?
options: Riders, please lock your bikes at the dock before leaving.
Riders please, lock your bikes at the dock before leaving.
Riders; please lock your bikes at the dock before leaving.
Riders, please, lock your bikes at the dock before leaving.
items.explanation: A word that directly addresses the reader, here riders, is set off with a comma. Placing the comma after please separates it from the verb it modifies. A semicolon needs a full clause on each side, and riders alone is not one. Commas on both sides of please cut the request into pieces.
